Subject: Recap & next steps — deployment mode (shared vs dedicated)

Hi Samir,

Thanks again for taking time today — really helpful to understand FinWave's high-throughput inference needs for the new fraud-detection feature. Quick recap and proposed next steps: 

What we heard
- Peak inference: ~1.2M requests/day, 99th pct latency target ~150ms for short prompts.
- Sensitive PII in payloads; SOC2 and VPC controls are required for production.
- Concerned about multi-tenant "noisy neighbor" effects and shared GPU interference.

Options we discussed
1) Hosted API (fastest) — good for quick proof-of-concept; comes with caching and isolation at the request layer but is shared infra.
2) Dedicated capacity — reserved GPU pools; predictable throughput and stronger isolation guarantees.
3) Private VPC/on-prem — full network isolation and KMS/HSM options for highly regulated data.

Questions we still have
- Do you need strict tenancy isolation (hardware-level) or is tenancy isolation + predictable SLOs sufficient?
- Are you planning to hit peak traffic within the next 60 days for the POC?

Proposed next steps
- I can loop in Priyom (solutions) on noisy-neighbor SLOs and isolation boundaries — he added some notes to this thread.
- Send over a short SLO/isolations primer and SOC2 summary (attached).
- Schedule a 30-min follow-up next week to walk through Dedicated capacity sizing and pricing.

Attachments: soc2-summary-2024.pdf

Hi Neha,

Thanks for the clear summary — appreciate it. A few clarifying points from our side: 

- For production we need predictable 99th pct latency and tight throughput guarantees; noisy neighbor events on shared infra are a hard no if they can cause latency spikes >200ms.
- We don't require dedicated physical hardware initially, but we do need guaranteed isolation (either dedicated capacity with tenant isolation or Private VPC with strict network controls).
- Timeline: want to start a POC in ~4–6 weeks, ramp to production in ~3 months.

Can Priyom outline the specific isolation boundaries Redwood offers on Dedicated (hardware pinning vs software tenancy) and what SLOs/RTOs you commit to for noisy neighbor incidents? Also please include any runbooks for incident escalation and mitigation — our security team will review.

Hi Samir — quick technical follow-up with concrete answers to the noisy-neighbor / isolation questions: 

Short answer:
- Dedicated capacity provides tenant-level isolation at the GPU-pool level (customers get reserved GPU instances and dedicated runtime pools). We do not promise single-tenant physical GPU pinning by default, but we can discuss options for hardware pinning for regulated workloads under Private deployment contracts.

What Dedicated includes (by default)
- Reserved GPU pools with capacity guarantees (minimum concurrent tokens/sec) and predictable scheduling — this avoids typical multi-tenant oversubscription spikes.
- Network isolation between tenant control planes and customer workloads (VPC peering or private link).
- KV cache partitioning and per-tenant batching lanes to avoid cross-tenant batch head-of-line blocking.
- SLA: committed 99th pct latency target for provisioned capacity; we provide a performance SLO for token latency (example: 99th < 180ms for models in the verified catalog at 512-token context under provisioned throughput). Exact numbers vary by model; we can run a baseline benchmark for your model.

Noisy-neighbor mitigation and runbook
- Continuous workload monitoring: token latency heatmaps and per-tenant queue depth alerts.
- Auto-shift policy: if a tenant's bursts threaten adjacent pools, we proactively migrate burst traffic to burst-capacity pools and throttle non-critical background work.
- Incident response: 15-min page escalation to on-call infra + 2-hr mitigation SLA for performance-impacting noisy-neighbor events for Dedicated customers (documented in the Dedicated contract).

Attachments: redwood-slos.pdf (short SLO summary + runbook excerpt)

Next steps we recommend
1) Run a 1-hour baseline benchmark on a representative workload (we can spin up a dedicated pool for this).
2) Confirm expected concurrency and peak tokens/sec so we can size the pool.
3) If you want, we can include a dedicated burst pool and an automatic fallback policy to Hosted API during capacity ramp.

Happy to jump on a quick call to walk through the benchmark plan.

—Priyom
